suggestive as preliminary evidence of specific plant-snail associations. Further investigations of absolute abundance of plants in relation to snail distribution will further support such findings. These results would also be enhanced by further investigation of other factors observed in this study that affect the distribution of snails since the Snail Kites tend to concentrate foraging efforts in areas of high prey abundance.¹ A more rigorous methodology including more quantitative measurements of these observed factors will improve available information on this subject since it is relatively unaddressed in available literature. It is a possibility that Snail Kites recognize limiting factors in Snail distribution (like vegetative thickness, heat, and plant associations). According to Bourne (1985), Kites generally avoid areas dense in floating vegetation and the majority of the time select the most profitable and efficient foraging site. From the suggestive plant-snail association in this study, it can be proposed that the snails themselves are selective within the habitat which puts even more foraging pressure on the specialist Kite, which is then amplified by habitat destruction that removes plants important to the snail population.

Ultimately, the selection of type and size of prey by the Snail Kite limits its diet, which may be secondarily limited by snail dependence on specific plant species. Therefore, the future success of the endangered Snail Kite will depend on the health of its habitat. Efforts to improve the management and conservation of wetland habitats should be further considered as one solution to the critical state of the Snail Kite.
